opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me most is that these models are, in a strange way, the first really capable systems we've built without understanding how they work. We train them, we see that they can write code, translate, reason through problems, and then if you ask "how is it actually doing that?" the honest answer for a long time was: we don't really know. We have the weights, every single number, but they don't explain themselves.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to close that gap by treating the model like an object of scientific study. Instead of only looking at inputs and outputs, you open it up and ask what the intermediate computations represent. What features is the model building internally? How do they combine across layers to produce an answer? The goal is something closer to a circuit diagram, or a biologist's map of an organism, than a black box with a behavior report attached.

Part of why I find it so compelling is that the answers are often surprising. You'd think a model just pattern-matches the next word, but when you trace its internals, you sometimes find it planning ahead, say thinking about the word it wants to rhyme with before writing the line. Or you find that it computes things like arithmetic in a way that's quite different from how it describes its own reasoning when you ask it. Those findings change your intuitions about what these systems are doing.

And beyond curiosity, there's a practical reason. As these models are deployed in more places, we want to know when they're being truthful, when they're making things up, and when they might do something we didn't intend. Behavioral testing can only take you so far, because you can't test every input. If you can understand the mechanisms, you have a much better shot at predicting behavior, catching failures, and building trust that's grounded in something real rather than just "it seemed fine in our evals."

So it's a mix of the scientific thrill, it's genuinely like discovering how a new kind of mind works, and the conviction that this understanding is going to matter a lot for making these systems safe and reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says mechanistic interpretability examines internal computations and can reveal behavior beyond simple next-word pattern matching. It does not connect this examination to grounding the debate over whether models merely match training data or generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that for most of the history of machine learning, we've been in this weird position where we build these systems, they work, and we have very little idea why. And for a long time that was sort of tolerable, because the models were doing narrow things, and you could evaluate them on a benchmark and move on. But with language models, the thing we've built is a system that does thousands of different tasks, that we interact with in natural language, that people are increasingly relying on for real decisions, and our main tool for understanding it is still basically to ask it questions and see what it says.

And the problem with that is that the model's explanation of its own behavior is just another output of the model. It's not privileged. If you ask a model why it gave a particular answer, you get a plausible-sounding story, but there's no guarantee that story has anything to do with the computation that actually happened. We've seen this concretely, cases where the model does the arithmetic one way internally and then describes doing it the textbook way, or where it works backwards from a hint it was given and then writes out a forward derivation as if it never saw the hint.

So what gets me excited about mechanistic interpretability is that it's the one approach that tries to go around that. Instead of asking the model, you look inside it. You treat it like a biological system almost, where you have this organism that wasn't designed by anyone in the usual sense, it grew out of a training process, and you want to figure out what its parts are and how they fit together. And the thing that's been surprising over the last couple of years is that this is actually tractable. We can find features, directions inside the model that correspond to human-understandable concepts, things like a specific person, or the notion of a bug in code, or a particular kind of sycophantic behavior. And more recently we can trace how those features connect to each other, how information flows from the input through these intermediate concepts to the output, and build what's essentially a circuit diagram for a specific behavior.

And once you can do that, a bunch of things open up. You can check whether the model's reasoning matches its explanation. You can find cases where the model knows something but doesn't say it, or says something it doesn't actually believe internally. You can see that when the model writes a rhyming poem it's actually planning the rhyme word ahead of time rather than just improvising token by token, which is not what a lot of people assumed. I think of it as the difference between judging a student by their answers versus being able to watch them work. The first one tells you whether they got it right this time. The second one tells you whether you should trust them next time.

I'd also say, to be fair about it, we're very early. The tools we have capture a fraction of what's going on, and they're expensive to use. But it's the first time I've felt like there's a real path from "this thing works" to "we understand why it works," and given how much we're starting to depend on these systems, I think that path matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes inspecting model internals and tracing features to understand behavior, but it does not connect mechanistic interpretability to the debate over whether language models merely match training data or generalize.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of moving from observing what a model does to understanding how it does it. We can ask a language model questions and evaluate its answers, but that leaves a lot of uncertainty about what’s happening internally. Two models might give the same answer for very different reasons.

Mechanistic interpretability tries to get at those reasons. Can we identify the internal representations and computations responsible for a particular behavior? And then, if we think we’ve found something, can we intervene on it and see whether the behavior changes in the way we predicted? That causal test is really appealing to me. It gives us a way to check an explanation instead of just telling a plausible story about the model.

There’s still a big gap between understanding a small piece of a model and understanding the whole system. But even partial progress could help us investigate failures and figure out why a model behaves differently in situations that look similar to us. That feels like a promising direction for making these systems more understandable and reliable.

r001.rationale: The response describes investigating internal representations and testing them causally, but does not connect mechanistic interpretability to debates about matching training data versus generalizing.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of moving from observing what a model does to understanding how it does it. We can test a language model on lots of examples, but that still leaves us inferring its behavior from the outside. Mechanistic interpretability asks whether we can look inside and identify the computations responsible for a particular response.

And the really interesting part is testing those explanations. If we think some internal feature is driving a behavior, can we intervene on it and change that behavior in a predictable way? That gives us a way to distinguish a plausible story from a causal explanation.

There’s still a lot of work to do. Understanding one mechanism doesn’t mean we understand the whole model. But even partial understanding could help us diagnose failures and build more reliable systems. That possibility—being able to investigate why something happened instead of only collecting more examples of it—is what I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response presents mechanistic interpretability as examining internal computations and testing causal explanations, but it does not connect that examination to the debate over whether language models merely match training data or generalize.
